newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech FinMin says monetary policy will be eased - TV.
newsitem.headline: Czech FinMin says monetary policy will be eased - TV.

text.p: A series of sweeping measures to jump-start the ailing Czech economy will include an easing of the central bank's monetary policy, Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik told Czech Television on Sunday.

Kocarnik said there will also be specific measures aimed at exporters, importers and industry, and encouraging citizens to save, but he gave no specific details on the measures, which are to be announced on April 16.
Speaking on the Nova television station on Sunday, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said some of the moves to be implemented would to help slow, but not eliminate wage growth.
"Real wages in the budgetary sphere went up by 12 percent in 1996 and that was too much," he said on a politcal debate programme.
"(But measures to be taken) will only slow down the growth of wages, not reduce them," he said adding wages should grow less than the 11.9 percent anticipated by the 1997 budget.
Klaus refused to give specifics on any of the measures, but he did say the package would contain both short- and long-term moves.
The short-term measures, he said, will cut budget expenses and add steps to complete the transformation of the economy.

Long-term measures will focus on the speedy completion of privatisation, improved capital market transparency, the seeking of new conditions to protect local markets and more severe prosecution of economic crimes, Klaus said.

Klaus and other ministers have recently been critical of the central bank's moves last June to tighten monetary policy, saying that the resulting slowdown in inflation has not been worth the price of a weakening in economic growth.
On Thursday, the Czech National Bank (CNB) and the government agreed to coordinate their policies.

The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom. But industrial and construction output have both declined for two consecutive months as the central bank moves continue to bite.
"(But) We are not in crisis," Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Sunday. "We are only at the crossroads considering which of the roads to take."
